Q: What is the difference between serializability and linearizability? A:

Serializability vs Linearizability

From Martin Kleppmann's Designing Data Intensive Applications (DDIA), in chapter 9 "Consistency and Consensus":

Serializability is an isolation property of transactions, where every transaction may read and write multiple objects (rows, documents, records). It guarantees that transactions behave the same as if they had executed in some serial order (each transaction running to completion before the next transaction starts). It is okay for that serial order to be different from the order in which transactions were actually run.

Linearizability is a recency guarantee on reads and writes of a register (an individual object). It doesn't group operations together into transactions, so it does not prevent problems such as write skew, unless you take additional measures such as materializing conflicts.

A database may provide both serializability and linearizability, and this combination is known as strict serializability or strong one-copy serializability (strong-1SR). Implementations of serializability based on two-phase locking or actual serial execution are typically linearizable.

However, serializable snapshot isolation is not linearizable: by design, it makes reads from a consistent snapshot, to avoid lock contention between readers and writers. The whole point of a consistent snapshot is that it does not include writes that are more recent than the snapshot, and thus reads from the snapshot are not linearizable.

As mentioned in another answer, serializability applies to transactions (= multiple registers), while linearizability applies to a single register (i.e. one row in the database).

Serializability

Serializability means that, when the database receives multiple transactions, it applies them as if they were applied one after the other (sequentially). This doesn't mean that the database actually applies them sequentially: for example, if two transactions affect independent rows, the database can execute them in parallel and the outcome will remain the same. The important thing is that the result must be the same as if the transactions were applied sequentially. Also, the order in which the database applies the transactions is not necessarily the same as the order in which it received them: this is why linearizability might be needed in addition to serializability.

Serializable isolation is the strongest isolation level in many databases. It prevents all race conditions.

Strategies for a database to provide serializability:

Strategy Pros Cons
Executing only one transaction at a time Simple to implement. Read-only queries can still be parallelized (since they do not modify the data). Avoids overhead of managing locks and can sometimes perform better than parallel queries. Throughput limited to that of a single CPU core. Limited to cases where the data is in-memory (too slow if disk access is needed). One slow transaction can stall all the others waiting. No interactive query (waiting for user input), which would block any other query.
Two-phase locking Transactions affecting independent rows can be parallelized. Uses pessimistic locking. Readers block writers and vice versa. Low performance due to overhead of managing locks. One slow transaction can stall other transactions affecting the same rows. Deadlocks.
Serializable Snapshot Isolation (SSI) Uses optimistic locking: transactions are not blocked. Read-only queries do not block at all. High-throughput thanks to multi-core parallelization. Transactions should remain small and fast to avoid being retried due to conflicts.

See chapter 7 "Transactions" of Martin Kleppmann's book for more details on serializability.

Linearizability

I would describe it this way: once a value has been written or read, all the subsequent reads, whichever the replica is, must return the same value or a more recent value, not an older one.

The example given in Kleppmann's book to illustrate the concept is a website announcing the result of a sport competition. This website uses a database with multiple read replicas. At the end of the competition, the result is added to the database. Alice reads the result from Replica A and sees who the winner is ("Hey, Germany has won the World Cup!"). Shortly after, Bob opens the website which this time reaches Replica B which hasn't received the final score yet ("Really? The website says they're still playing"). In that scenario, the data is not linearizable because Bob read the score after Alice, but received an older value.

In the case where a read happens concurrently with a write on the same register, for the register to be linearizable:

  1. The newly written value can be read any time between the moment the write operation starts and the moment it ends, but no later.
  2. Once the newly written value has been read once, all subsequent reads must return the new value as well.

ASCII-style illustrations: in the illustrations below, [---] represents the duration of a transaction. [ is the invocation (start), and ] is the response (completion/return).

Linearizable system:

Write(B)             [------- WRITE OPERATION -------]
                         ^
                         |
                 Linearization Point
           (The moment the change "happens")

Read 1          [---] Returns A (Legal: finished before the flip)

Read 2                  [---] Returns B (Legal: started after the flip)

Read 3              [-----------] Returns B (Legal: overlaps flip, picks B)

Non-linearizable system:

Write(B)             [------- WRITE OPERATION -------]

Read 1 (Replica 1)       [---] Returns B (Sees the update early)

Read 2 (Replica 2)               [---] Returns A (ILLEGAL: Read 2 started AFTER Read 1 finished, but saw older data)

See chapter 9 "Consistency and Consensus" of Martin Kleppmann's book for more details on linearizability.
